lesson.title: Have You Earned the Attack?
lesson.hook: The same ball can offer a different opportunity. Read the whole situation before you choose.
lesson.tomorrow: Before attacking an opening, check whether you have arrived with room to swing. If you are still chasing the ball, favour margin and recovery.
lesson.cue: See the space. Check your arrival.

pro.label: Annacone · Spot the invitation
pro.moment: In Annacone’s attacking lesson, the invitation is a short ball. His player uses the approach to create a volley they can finish. That sequence matters: first recognise the opportunity, then build the easier shot. Wanting to attack does not create the invitation.
pro.read: Your next point: an empty corner is useful when you can reach the ball in control. Check your arrival and contact before choosing the attack.

steps.name: Choose your plan
steps.sit: Their reply comes to your forehand. The far side is open.
opts: Drive into the open court, with margin
steps.payoff: Arrive with room, then use the opening.
steps.principle: Read your arrival as well as the ball and the opponent.
steps.why: You have reached your preparation position while the opponent is still across the court. A controlled drive into the space can apply pressure. A deeper, higher reply is also reasonable; you do not have to force an attack.
steps.take: Arrive with room, then use the opening.

lines.A: Room to prepare and an opening: pressure is available.
lines.B: A sound reset; you also had an opportunity to apply pressure.

steps.name: Choose your plan
steps.sit: The same incoming ball. The same opening. Watch this point.
opts: Drive into the open court, with margin
steps.payoff: An opening is useful only if your arrival lets you use it.
steps.principle: Read your arrival as well as the ball and the opponent.
steps.why: The ball and opponent have not changed. Your starting position has: you are still crossing to the ball. Lift with margin and recover instead of forcing a drive just because the far court is empty.
steps.take: An opening is useful only if your arrival lets you use it.

lines.A: The space is tempting, but your arrival makes this harder to control.
lines.B: Give yourself margin and time to recover.

steps.name: Choose your plan
steps.sit: A new rally. What would you choose here?
opts: Drive into the open court, with margin
steps.payoff: Read your arrival again; the previous answer is not a rule.
steps.principle: Read your arrival as well as the ball and the opponent.
steps.why: Here you are being pulled wide and the opponent is central. Height and depth give you a better chance to recover. This is a different ball and court position, but the same readiness check.
steps.take: Read your arrival again; the previous answer is not a rule.

lines.A: Height and depth help you work your way back.
lines.B: Still moving wide, with no clear opening: forcing pressure adds risk.

drill.name: Call the plan
drill.how: With a partner, vary the feed and your starting position. Before contact, call “pressure” or “buy time”. Afterwards, compare the call with your arrival, the ball and their position. Keep a useful cue; a won or lost point alone does not settle the decision.

readiness.evidence: Arrived before the bounce; room to prepare.
Still moving across as the ball arrives.
Wide, still moving, with the opponent central.
